```js

```
rewrite.hint: length counts storage units, not what a reader would call characters.
rewrite.explanation: String.prototype.length is the number of UTF-16 code units. "hello" needs five of them, so there length happens to equal the character count, but an emoji outside the Basic Multilingual Plane is stored as a surrogate pair and reports 2 - while [..."😀"].length is 1, because iteration walks code points. This is why length is the wrong measure for a character limit on user-entered text.

rewrite.hint: Level by level means every node one step away is handled before anything two steps away. Which structure preserves arrival order?
rewrite.explanation: BFS holds its frontier in a FIFO queue: dequeue a node, enqueue its unvisited neighbors, so everything at distance k is processed before anything at distance k+1 - on A to {B,C}, B to {D,E}, C to {F} the visit order is A, B, C, D, E, F. Replace the queue with a stack and the same code becomes DFS, visiting A, B, D, E, C, F; in-order traversal and backtracking are likewise stack- or recursion-driven, so they dive deep before going wide.

rationale: The queue-to-BFS link is one of the most useful facts in the level, but half the option set is from unrelated topics.
evidence: node: the same traversal code visited A,B,C,D,E,F with a queue and A,B,D,E,C,F with a stack

rewrite.question: A sliding window needs to add items at one end and drop them from either end as it advances. Which structure supports that in O(1) per operation?
options: A double-ended queue
A singly linked list with only a head pointer
A binary search tree
A hash set
rewrite.hint: Both ends have to be cheap here, not just one. Which structure keeps a handle on each?
rewrite.explanation: A deque keeps handles on both head and tail, so adding or removing at either end is O(1) - what a sliding-window maximum or a capacity-limited undo/redo pair needs. A singly linked list with only a head can drop the front cheaply but needs O(n) to reach the tail, a search tree costs O(log n) per operation, and a hash set has no ends at all.

rationale: As written the learner only has to unpack the name; asking which structure meets a two-ended requirement tests what a deque is for.
evidence: knowledge: a deque supports O(1) insertion and removal at both ends; a head-only singly linked list needs O(n) to reach the tail

rewrite.hint: Ask which scenario cares about arrival order rather than about the most recent item.
rewrite.explanation: Tasks that must run in the order they arrived are FIFO, which a queue models directly: enqueue on arrival, dequeue to run. The other three are all LIFO - nested parentheses need the most recent unmatched opening bracket, reversing a string consumes characters newest-first, and recursion is the call stack itself - so recognizing 'most recent' against 'longest waiting' decides every one of them.

defects: 'It allows duplicate values' is a non-answer

options: It reuses freed front slots instead of shifting elements

It keeps the elements in sorted order

rewrite.hint: The slots freed at the front are still there but stranded. Ask how wrapping the index reaches them.
rewrite.explanation: Head and tail indexes advance modulo the capacity, so a slot freed at the front is reused once the tail wraps around and no element ever moves. Counting element moves for n enqueues followed by n dequeues gives 500,500 for a shifting array queue at n = 1000, against 2,000 for a circular buffer. Wrapping does not create capacity - a full circular queue still has to resize or reject - and it needs both indexes, not fewer.

rationale: A genuinely useful implementation fact and the natural follow-on to rm-dsa-51; one option is filler and the explanation carries no cost comparison.

defects: hint is the generic shape-based fallback

rewrite.hint: There is no address arithmetic available here. Ask how you actually get from the head to position k.
rewrite.explanation: Nodes sit wherever they were allocated, so position k is reached only by following k next-pointers from the head: on a 100-node list, index 50 cost 50 hops and index 99 cost 99. That is O(n) in the worst case, against O(1) for an array's address computation. What the list buys in exchange is O(1) insertion and removal once you already hold the node, with no shifting.

rationale: Correct, precisely scoped ('by position'), and the counterpart to rm-dsa-17; only the hint is boilerplate.

rewrite.explanation: A singly linked node holds its value plus a reference to the next node, with the last node's reference null - that chain is the whole structure. Storing an index instead would require the contiguous array a linked list exists to avoid, and every insertion would have to renumber all the nodes that follow, turning an O(1) splice into O(n).

Nothing else moves, which is the mirror image of an array, where inserting at the front shifts every existing element and costs O(n).

options: A reference to the previous node

rewrite.hint: A singly linked list can only move one way. Ask what a node needs in order to step backward.
rewrite.explanation: Each node keeps prev as well as next, so traversal runs in both directions and a node you already hold can be removed in O(1) - a singly linked list has to walk from the head to find the predecessor first. The cost is one extra pointer per node and two links to keep consistent on every insertion and removal, which is where doubly linked list bugs come from.

rationale: Correct and a good close to the level, but two options are filler and the explanation gives the benefit without the price.
evidence: knowledge: a doubly linked node stores next and prev, enabling O(1) removal of a held node and bidirectional traversal
